iv-ap-01.a.text: The organization's proprietary knowledge is trained directly into the model's weights through additional training rounds, becoming a permanent part of what the model "knows."
iv-ap-01.a.why: Baking domain data into the weights means the model inherits whatever memorization or leakage risk that data carries — a synthetic-data generator adapted this way on production records can still leak traces of the originals even after anonymization, and using student-specific data the same way creates its own breach exposure.
iv-ap-01.b.text: The organization's proprietary knowledge stays in an external, separately maintained store and is pulled in only at the moment each question is asked.
iv-ap-01.b.why: Nothing about this knowledge is learned by the model itself — it's fetched fresh per query, which is exactly why it can reflect this month's guidance without a single retraining run. The adaptation choice made here is what determines the assurance burden the team ends up owning.

iv-ap-02.a.text: Fetches the current policy documents to ground a single answer, which a human then reads and acts on.
iv-ap-02.a.why: The system's job stops at producing a well-grounded answer; every consequential action downstream is still a human's to take.
iv-ap-02.b.text: Plans a multi-step task on its own and executes actions across booking and payment tools, with minimal human review at each step.
iv-ap-02.b.why: Autonomy of action, not just autonomy of answer, is the new governance surface here: when a deployer lets a system act rather than merely inform, the deployer answers directly if the agent causes harm or misleads anyone — this calls for action scoping, human-in-the-loop thresholds, and full action logs, none of which a purely retrieval-grounded assistant needs.

iv-ap-03.a.text: The organization can read, modify and redistribute the model's own weights and code, and run it entirely on infrastructure it controls.
iv-ap-03.a.why: Inspectability is the whole trade: you get to audit the algorithm yourself and avoid depending on one vendor's roadmap, but you also inherit the internal burden of checking licenses, training-data provenance and your own security testing.
iv-ap-03.b.text: The organization can only call the model through an API and never sees the weights, but the vendor backs it with support contracts, incident response and indemnities.
iv-ap-03.b.why: You trade inspection rights for contract-backed guarantees — and the strategic cost of that trade is recorded as the top risk of this path: once workflows are built around one vendor's API, switching away later gets expensive.

iv-ap-04.a.text: The base model is compressed and reshaped — parameters pruned, precision reduced, a lightweight adapter layered on — to cut cost and latency for edge or high-volume use.
iv-ap-04.a.why: Shrinking or reshaping the artifact this way can quietly move its decision boundaries and reduce interpretability, so accuracy, fairness and robustness all need to be re-checked after every such change, not assumed to carry over unchanged.
iv-ap-04.b.text: The vendor's model runs unmodified, exactly as shipped, backed only by human review and other controls layered on around it.
iv-ap-04.b.why: Nothing about the artifact itself has changed, so governance leans on the vendor's own documentation and on compensating controls like human review rather than on re-validating the model's internals.

iv-ap-05.a.text: A credit-scoring system predicts or classifies from structured inputs; its risks are bias against certain groups and accuracy that quietly degrades as the underlying data drifts.
iv-ap-05.a.why: Predicting or classifying a known category from structured features is this profile's failure mode — familiar bias and drift risks that fairness testing and monitoring are built to catch.
iv-ap-05.b.text: A drafting assistant produces brand-new text, images or code from a prompt; its risks are hallucination, copyright exposure and convincingly wrong output.
iv-ap-05.b.why: Creating content that didn't exist before opens a different risk surface entirely — hallucination and provenance, not the bias-and-drift profile that governs a prediction-only system.

iv-ap-06.a.text: A vendor's model is used exactly as delivered; the team's job is to validate it against its own performance and fairness standards and document any gaps.
iv-ap-06.a.why: Governance here leans almost entirely on vendor transparency plus compensating controls — the team never touches the model's internals, so its obligations stop at validation and documentation.
iv-ap-06.b.text: A general-purpose model is retrained on the organization's own labeled data until it reproduces a specific, desired behavior.
iv-ap-06.b.why: The moment an organization retrains the model, governance treats the result as a new system: fairness and robustness testing must be repeated from scratch, and — compared with using a vendor's model as delivered — the organization now carries increased legal liability of its own.

iv-ap-07.a.text: A support chatbot takes in written questions and produces written answers only, with no other input channel to reason over.
iv-ap-07.a.why: Text-only in, text-only out — the governance concerns here are hallucination, biased phrasing and jailbreak-style prompt attacks, none of which involve a second modality.
iv-ap-07.b.text: A claims tool weighs a damage photograph together with the adjuster's written notes before producing a single combined judgment.
iv-ap-07.b.why: Combining channels adds a risk a text-only system never faces: false correlations between an image and the text next to it, and the need to show which input actually drove the output.

iv-ap-08.a.text: A narrow classifier handles one task on a tight compute budget, retrains quickly, and traces its outputs back to inputs with little effort.
iv-ap-08.a.why: A compact, narrow system is cheap to re-test and easy to explain — the cost is that it can underperform once the environment gets more variable than what it was built for.
iv-ap-08.b.text: A broad foundation system generalizes across many tasks it was never specifically trained for, at the cost of heavier compute governance and a bigger attack surface.
iv-ap-08.b.why: Breadth bought through scale means the system can tackle unfamiliar domains zero-shot, but it also needs compute quotas, red-teaming and drift monitoring that a narrow system doesn't.

iv-ap-09.a.text: Every source the model drew on during a session gets logged for audit, and any personal data passing through the connected corpus must be redacted before it's ever shown to the model.
iv-ap-09.a.why: Audit logging and PII redaction across an external corpus are governance obligations that simply don't exist for a model with no live data pipeline attached — this path's assurance burden lives in the plumbing, not the weights.
iv-ap-09.b.text: The vendor's model is used exactly as delivered, and the fastest path to a working pilot is chosen precisely because no new training data or pipeline needs to be built first.
iv-ap-09.b.why: Speed is the entire appeal here — no retraining, no new data plumbing — but governance treats that speed as a debt: the model is presumed high-risk until validated against this organization's own performance and fairness standards, since nothing about it was built with this deployment in mind.

iv-ap-10.a.text: The same base model comes out smaller and cheaper to run after compression, without a single new fact having been added to it.
iv-ap-10.a.why: This path targets footprint, not knowledge — but shrinking or reshaping the artifact can still move its decision boundaries, so accuracy and fairness need re-checking even though nothing "new" was taught.
iv-ap-10.b.text: The same base model comes out the same size, but now reliably reproduces a specialist behavior it never had access to before, learned from curated examples.
iv-ap-10.b.why: This path targets behavior and knowledge, not footprint — and because that new behavior was learned from the organization's own data, governance now treats the result as a new system requiring its own testing, not a resized copy of the old one.
